title: Reproducible Research Pipelines with R and Quarto
text: Examples of what you can make with a little R and Quarto, where text, code, tables, figures and references sit in one file and are rebuilt with one command. They come from a seminar I taught at the University of Freiburg. New to this? Start with the guide R and Quarto: a short start.

title: R and Quarto: a short start
text:
This page grew out of the software tutorials of a seminar I taught at the University of Freiburg in the 2024/25 winter term, Reproducible research pipelines with R and Quarto. In it, Master’s students in economics took conflict event data from the raw files to clean data, maps, estimates and a finished report. What is useful beyond the seminar is kept here, rewritten as a short start.
It is for former participants who want to look something up, for anyone I have sent here, and for anyone who has just finished an R course and wants to write a first report in Quarto. If that is you, skip ahead to Quarto.

title: R and Quarto: a short start
text:
Why work this way
A reproducible pipeline means that every number, table and figure comes from code, and that one command rebuilds the whole document from the raw data:

raw data → R code → Quarto document → web page · Word · PDF · slides

Three habits follow from it:

Never edit data by hand. Keep the raw files as you got them and make every change in code.
Never copy a result into the text. Numbers, tables and figures are computed where they appear.
Keep everything in plain text. Scripts and Quarto files are text, so version control with Git can track every change.

The pay-off comes the second time round: when the data are updated or a referee asks for another specification, you rerun instead of redo, and text and results cannot drift apart. Plain text also suits coding agents, which can read, run and change a project like this.

title: R and Quarto: a short start
text:
Set up once

Install R, an editor and Quarto. RStudio Desktop is the usual editor and comes with Quarto; Positron is Posit’s newer one. A separate Quarto install keeps Quarto up to date.
Make one folder per project. In RStudio, File › New Project creates the folder and an .Rproj file; open the project by double-clicking that file. R then starts in the project folder, so every path can be relative to it and the project runs on any computer:
my-project/
├── my-project.Rproj
├── data/             raw data, never edited by hand
├── report.qmd        text and code
└── references.bib    bibliography
births <- read.csv("data/births.csv")    # relative path: works anywhere
# setwd("C:/Users/me/Desktop/project")   # works only on your computer
Start each session clean. Under Tools › Global Options › General, untick Restore .RData into workspace at startup and set Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never. Restart R now and then (Session › Restart R) and run your code from the top: if it still works, your results come from your code and not from objects left over in memory.
Install a package once, load it in every script. install.packages("dplyr") downloads a package, library(dplyr) loads it. If you need to rerun a project years later, renv records the package versions it used.

title: R and Quarto: a short start
text:
The R you need first
The best free introduction is R for Data Science (Wickham et al. 2023), the seminar’s main reference. This section runs one small pipeline on data that come with R, so you can paste each step into the R console and get the same result.

Objects and functions

x <- c(2.9, 3.4, 3.1)   # <- assigns; c() combines values into a vector
mean(x)                 # a function applied to x

[1] 3.133333


Everything you work with is an object with a name, and you do things to objects with functions. ?mean opens the help page of a function.


Data

library(MASS)       # comes with R and contains the data set birthwt
head(birthwt, 3)

   low age lwt race smoke ptl ht ui ftv  bwt
85   0  19 182    2     0   0  0  1   0 2523
86   0  33 155    3     0   0  0  0   3 2551
87   0  20 105    1     1   0  0  0   1 2557


birthwt holds 189 births at a US hospital in 1986, used in a textbook on logistic regression (Hosmer and Lemeshow 1989): the birth weight in grams (bwt), whether the mother smoked during pregnancy (smoke, coded 0 and 1), her age (age), her weight in pounds (lwt) and more (see ?birthwt). Your own data you read from a file:
dat <- read.csv("data/my-data.csv")              # text file, comma-separated
dat <- readxl::read_excel("data/my-data.xlsx")   # Excel
dat <- haven::read_dta("data/my-data.dta")       # Stata


Clean

library(dplyr)

births <- birthwt |>
  mutate(
    smoker    = factor(smoke, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    weight_kg = bwt / 1000,
    mother_kg = lwt * 0.4536
  ) |>
  select(weight_kg, smoker, age, mother_kg)

head(births, 3)

   weight_kg smoker age mother_kg
85     2.523     No  19   82.5552
86     2.551     No  33   70.3080
87     2.557    Yes  20   47.6280


The pipe |> hands the result of one step to the next: take birthwt, then add variables with mutate(), then keep four of them with select(). Turning a 0/1 code into a labelled factor makes every table, figure and model that follows easier to read.


Summarise

births |>
  group_by(smoker) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(weight_kg), sd = sd(weight_kg)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)



Table 1: Birth weight in kg by whether the mother smoked during pregnancy.






smoker
n
mean
sd




No

Yes

group_by() and summarise() compute statistics by group, and knitr::kable() formats the result as a table, Table 1. For tables ready for a paper, see gtsummary, common in medicine, and modelsummary, common in economics.


Plot

library(ggplot2)
set.seed(2024)   # the jitter below is random: fix it to get the same figure

ggplot(births, aes(x = smoker, y = weight_kg)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Mother smoked during pregnancy", y = "Birth weight (kg)") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Birth weight by whether the mother smoked during pregnancy.





A ggplot is built in layers: the data and which variable goes where (aes()), then the geometry (boxes, points), then labels and a theme. In Figure 1 each birth is a point on top of the boxplot.


Model

fit <- lm(weight_kg ~ smoker + age + mother_kg, data = births)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = weight_kg ~ smoker + age + mother_kg, data = births)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-2.07097 -0.43156  0.01295  0.52170  1.81167 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  2.362495   0.300683   7.857 3.12e-13 ***
smokerYes   -0.269257   0.105801  -2.545   0.0117 *  
age          0.007154   0.009925   0.721   0.4719    
mother_kg    0.008853   0.003791   2.335   0.0206 *  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.7088 on 185 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.07039,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.05531 
F-statistic: 4.669 on 3 and 185 DF,  p-value: 0.003606


In these data, babies of mothers who smoked weighed on average 269 g less than babies of mothers of the same age and weight who did not smoke. That number is not typed into this page: inline code in the page’s source computes it, so it would change with the data. Whether it is the effect of smoking is a question of research design, not of code; Huntington-Klein (2021) is a readable introduction to causal inference with observational data.

title: R and Quarto: a short start
text:
Quarto
Quarto turns a plain-text file that mixes text and code into a finished document. A .qmd file has three parts: a header between two --- lines, written in YAML; text, written in Markdown; and code chunks, which run when the document is rendered. Here is a complete report built from the pipeline above. Save the two files in one folder and render the first:


report.qmd

---
title: "Smoking and birth weight"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format:
  html: default
  docx: default
  typst:              # PDF, without installing LaTeX
    citeproc: true    # cite as in HTML and Word
bibliography: references.bib
execute:
  echo: false
---

```{r}
#| include: false
library(MASS)       # contains the data set birthwt
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

births <- birthwt |>
  mutate(smoker    = factor(smoke, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
         weight_kg = bwt / 1000)

fit <- lm(weight_kg ~ smoker, data = births)
diff_g <- round(-1000 * coef(fit)[["smokerYes"]])
```

## Data

The data are `r nrow(births)` births at a US hospital in 1986 [@hosmer1989].
@tbl-means shows birth weight by whether the mother smoked during pregnancy.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-means
#| tbl-cap: "Birth weight (kg) by smoking during pregnancy."
births |>
  group_by(smoker) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(weight_kg), sd = sd(weight_kg)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

## Results

Babies of mothers who smoked weighed on average `r diff_g` g less
(@fig-weight).

```{r}
#| label: fig-weight
#| fig-cap: "Birth weight by smoking during pregnancy."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(births, aes(x = smoker, y = weight_kg)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Mother smoked", y = "Birth weight (kg)")
```

## References



references.bib

@book{hosmer1989,
  author    = {Hosmer, David W. and Lemeshow, Stanley},
  title     = {Applied Logistic Regression},
  year      = {1989},
  publisher = {Wiley},
  address   = {New York}
}


Render

In RStudio, click Render (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K); in Positron, Preview.
In a terminal, quarto render report.qmd makes all three formats in the header, quarto render report.qmd --to docx makes only the Word file, and quarto preview report.qmd renders again each time you save.

The same file becomes a web page, a Word document and a PDF, each with Table 1, Figure 1, the numbers in the text, the citation and the list of references in place.


What each part does

Header. Title, author, date, the output formats and their options, the bibliography. echo: false hides the code in the output, which suits a report; leave it out for a tutorial like this page.
Chunk options. Lines starting with #| set options for one chunk: include: false runs the chunk but shows nothing, label names it, and fig-cap and tbl-cap add captions.
Inline code. `r nrow(births)` writes the number of births into the sentence; when the data change, the text changes with them.
Cross-references. A chunk labelled fig-… becomes a numbered figure and one labelled tbl-… a numbered table; @fig-weight in the text becomes “Figure 1”, with a link in the web page. Equations and sections work the same way (more).
Citations. [@hosmer1989] cites the entry with that key in references.bib, and the list of references goes at the end. Reference managers export .bib files; for Zotero, the Better BibTeX plugin keeps the file in sync. A citation style such as csl: apa.csl sets the format.



One source, many formats
Each of the seminar’s four assignments used another format; together they cover most of what you need:








Format
In the header
Good for




Web page
html
sharing as a link, or as one file with embed-resources: true


Word
docx
co-authors who edit in Word; reference-doc applies your template


PDF
typst, or pdf
papers and theses; pdf uses LaTeX, installed once with quarto install tinytex


Slides
revealjs
talks: each ## heading starts a new slide



Larger projects are websites, like this one, and books, like my thesis template; manuscripts bundle a paper with the notebooks behind it. When code takes long to run, freeze keeps its results until the code changes (more).

title: R and Quarto: a short start
text:
Practise
The seminar’s assignments make a good path through your own data, or through one of the data sets that come with R (data() lists them):

A web page with a few of the data steps above and two or three references.
A PDF with a figure and a table, both cross-referenced in the text.
Slides with an interactive figure or table, made for instance with plotly or DT.
One source, three outputs: the same file as web page, PDF and Word.

title: R and Quarto: a short start
text:
Going further
The seminar’s topics, and where to continue:

R and cleaning data: R for Data Science, above all its chapters on tidy data, joins, factors and dates. The Big Book of R lists hundreds of free books on R.
Figures: the ggplot2 extensions gallery, and Vincent Arel-Bundock on consistent figures in Quarto.
Maps and georeferenced data: Geocomputation with R.
Effects and research design: The Effect (Huntington-Klein 2021) and Scott Cunningham’s Causal Inference; Carlisle Rainey on equivalence tests, for arguing that an effect is negligible rather than merely not significant.
Workflow: What They Forgot to Teach You About R on projects and paths, Happy Git and GitHub for the useR on version control, and Frank Harrell’s R Workflow for reproducible clinical research. LSE’s Data for Data Scientists is a full course.
More Quarto: Emil Hvitfeldt’s Slidecraft 101 on slides, Cameron Patrick’s PDF formatting tips for theses, and a guide to effect sizes and confidence intervals written as a Quarto book.
Statistics: Richard McElreath’s Statistical Rethinking lectures.
A thesis topic that matters: Effective Thesis.

Once this workflow feels familiar, much of the routine can be handed to an AI agent: see Coding agents with GitHub.

Helpline research






NoteInteractive Figure: Conversation Topics in German Helpline Calls






TelefonSeelsorgeNummer gegen Kummer · youthNummer gegen Kummer · parents




                            
                                            






                            
                                            






                            
                                            





Deviation of conversation topics from their 2019 baseline, in percentage points, for calls to Germany’s two nationwide helplines for young people. Each tab uses that helpline’s own topic taxonomy rather than a harmonised one, so the categories differ between them: TelefonSeelsorge, the country’s largest helpline, records 41 topics for its adult callers, while Nummer gegen Kummer records 88 finer-grained ones, split here into its youth line (callers under 20) and its parent line (callers 20 and over).
Hover any line for the topic, the deviation that week and, for Nummer gegen Kummer, the broader category it belongs to; click a line to highlight it and name it above the plot. Based on some three million calls between January 2019 and May 2022.









NoteInteractive Figure: US Helpline Calls by State







                            
                                            


Each grey line is one US state; the mauve line is the nationwide weekly average. Calls are shown as deviations from each state’s own average over the period, so states of very different size can share one scale, and the two helplines get their own panel because they swing by very different amounts. Hover any line to identify the state, or click it to highlight that state in both panels and name it above the plot. Source data for Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 6, covering January 2020 to March 2021.

Political economy






NoteInteractive Figure: Terror Groups, 1860-1950







                            
                                            


Each marker is one terror group, placed at the city where it formed; hover for its name, ideology and years of activity. The two social-revolutionary ideologies the paper is about — anarchist and leftist — are drawn in colour; the remaining ideologies recede into greys but are all still shown and named on hover. Drag to pan and use the buttons at the top right to zoom — useful for the dense European cluster. Groups from the same city are fanned out slightly so they stay distinguishable, and present-day borders are drawn for orientation only.

title: Coding agents with GitHub
text:
A coding agent is an AI assistant that works inside your project rather than in a chat window. It reads your files, runs R and Quarto, changes code and text, and checks the result, for instance by rendering a report and reading the errors. Paired with Git and GitHub, every change it makes is recorded, and you can read it, discuss it, undo it or keep it.
This page describes how I work this way on this website, my teaching materials and research code, and how to set it up for a project like the one in R and Quarto: a short start.

title: Coding agents with GitHub
text:
What you need

A GitHub repository for your project. A repository is a project folder under version control: Git records every change with a message, and GitHub keeps a copy online where you can browse it, compare versions and review changes. Private repositories are free. If Git is new to you, Happy Git and GitHub for the useR explains the one-time setup, and from an RStudio project usethis::use_git() and usethis::use_github() do the rest.
A coding agent. I use Claude Code, from Anthropic. It runs in a terminal, in VS Code and JetBrains editors, in a desktop app, and in the browser at claude.ai/code, where each session runs in the cloud on a copy of your repository. OpenAI’s Codex and GitHub’s Copilot coding agent work along the same lines. These tools generally need a paid plan.

In the browser, the agent works in a cloud environment of its own and installs what it needs there, and your computer can be off. On your computer, it uses what you have installed. Either way, what the agent reads is sent to its provider, which matters for your data (see what stays with you).

title: Coding agents with GitHub
text:
The workflow

Describe the project once, in a short file in the repository’s main folder that the agent reads at the start of every session (see the next section).
Give one task per session, in plain words: the goal, who it is for, and what done looks like.
Let the agent work on a branch. It makes its changes on a separate branch, renders and checks them, commits them with messages that say why, and pushes the branch to GitHub. Your main branch stays as it was.
Review. Read the changes on GitHub, where a pull request shows every changed line; render the branch yourself; ask questions or for changes in the same session.
Merge the branch into main when you are satisfied, and publish if the project is a report or a website.
Update the instructions. When the agent gets something wrong twice, add a line to them, so the next session starts knowing it.

This page was written that way: in a cloud session with my website’s repository, on its own branch, and reviewed by me before it was merged.

title: Coding agents with GitHub
text:
A file of instructions
Claude Code reads a file called CLAUDE.md; Codex, Copilot and most other agents read AGENTS.md, a shared format. Keep it short and concrete: how to build and check the project, its conventions, and what to ask about first. For a thesis in R and Quarto it could start like this:


CLAUDE.md

# Project notes

Master's thesis on [topic]. Text in Quarto (.qmd files), analysis in R.

## Build and check
- `quarto render` builds the thesis as PDF and web version into _book/.
- Render after every change; fix all errors and warnings before committing.
- `Rscript R/01_clean.R` rebuilds the clean data from data/raw/.

## Conventions
- Paths relative to the project folder; never setwd().
- tidyverse style with the |> pipe; one numbered script per step in R/.
- No numbers typed into the text: use inline R.
- British English, short sentences.

## Data
- data/raw/ holds the original files: never change them, never commit them
  (they are listed in .gitignore).
- Never print individual records.

## Ask before
- changing the sample, a variable definition or a model;
- deleting files or rewriting Git history.

In Claude Code, the /init command drafts such a file from your repository; shorten the draft and add your own rules. Rules about the statistics belong here too. The instructions in the repository of my journal club talk, for example, say: “report both models and the fixed validation split. Do not select a model or split because it yields a stronger signal” (AGENTS.md).
To serve several agents from one file, write AGENTS.md and start CLAUDE.md with the line @AGENTS.md, which imports it (more).

title: Coding agents with GitHub
text:
Prompts that work
Write as you would to a capable research assistant who has not seen the project: the goal, the context, and how you will judge the result. Ask for a check at the end and for a short note on anything left undone. For example:

Turn analysis.R into a Quarto report, report.qmd, that renders to HTML and Word. Hide the code in the output, put the numbers in the text with inline R, and cross-reference the figures. Render both formats and fix any errors.
Add a Table 1 by treatment group with gtsummary and refer to it in the results section.
Set up my thesis from the template in the GitHub repository valentinklotzbuecher/ufr_thesis, with my name and title and three empty chapters: Introduction, Data, Results.
Review R/03_models.R for mistakes such as wrong variables, silently dropped missing values or factor coding. Don’t change anything; list what you find with line numbers.
Explain what R/02_merge.R does, step by step, for someone new to dplyr.

For a larger change, ask for a plan first and agree on it before any code is written. Keep tasks small: a session that does one thing is easier to review than one that does five.

title: Coding agents with GitHub
text:
What stays with you

The decisions. The research question, the analysis plan, the sample, the model and what the results mean. An agent will propose answers to all of them; they are yours to make and to defend.
The checking. Read every change before you merge it, and rerun the analysis yourself. Agents are fast and sound sure of themselves when they are wrong: they misread a variable, or make a failing check pass by loosening it.
The data. Keep identifiable personal data, such as patient data, out of the repository and out of the agent’s reach, and follow your institution’s rules. A line in CLAUDE.md is a request, not a lock. Where the real data cannot be shared, the agent can write and test the code on synthetic data with the same structure, and you run it on the real data yourself.
The rules on AI use. Universities, journals and employers have them. Check what applies, and say how you used AI: in a thesis, usually in the declaration of independent work.

In a study I co-authored, AI-assisted teams assessed the reproducibility of published research better than AI-led teams, but not better than human-only teams.
